text: Environmental samples have a stronger geographic gradient in AlphaEarth cosine distance than human-associated samples: 3.4x versus 2.0x.
quote: AlphaEarth embeddings encode geographic/environmental signal, but the strength depends on the sample source. For **environmental samples** (Soil, Marine, Freshwater, Extreme, Plant), nearby genomes (<100 km) have mean cosine distance 0.27, rising to 0.90 at intercontinental distances (>10,000 km) — a **3.4x ratio**. For **human-associated samples** (gut, clinical, other), the gradient is flatter: 0.37 nearby to 0.75 far — only a **2.0x ratio**.
heading: 1. Environmental samples show 3.4x stronger geographic signal than human-associated samples

text: The report interprets the flatter human-associated gradient as an urban-imagery effect and cautions that the pooled 2.0x curve blends distinct groups.
quote: This reflects the fact that hospitals and clinics worldwide share similar satellite imagery (urban built environment), so human-associated genomes have more homogeneous embeddings regardless of geography. Environmental samples, from genuinely diverse landscapes, show much stronger geographic differentiation. The pooled "All samples" curve (2.0x ratio) is a blend of these two signals, dominated by the 38% human-associated fraction.
heading: 1. Environmental samples show 3.4x stronger geographic signal than human-associated samples

text: In 50,000 pairs with good-quality coordinates, embedding distance rose with geographic distance, most strongly below 2,000 km, then plateaued beyond 5,000 km.
quote: Across all 50,000 sampled genome pairs (using only good-quality coordinates), there is a clear monotonic relationship between geographic distance and embedding cosine distance. The relationship is strongest at short distances (<2,000 km) and plateaus at intercontinental scales (>5,000 km), suggesting the embeddings capture local environmental conditions (climate, vegetation, land use) that are spatially autocorrelated.
heading: 2. AlphaEarth embeddings encode real geographic signal — not noise

text: The report supplies mean cosine distance and pair count for seven geographic-distance bins, from 0.41 among 231 pairs at <100 km to 0.82 among 16,107 pairs at 10K–20K km.
heading: 2. AlphaEarth embeddings encode real geographic signal — not noise

text: Of 83,287 embedded genomes, 38% are human-associated; Soil, Marine, and Freshwater each account for 7%. The report attributes the skew to clinical sequencing and metadata availability.
quote: 38% of the 83,287 genomes with AlphaEarth embeddings are human-associated: Human clinical (16,390; 20%), Human gut (13,466; 16%), and Human other (1,669; 2%). Environmental categories are much smaller: Soil (6,073; 7%), Marine (5,850; 7%), Freshwater (5,840; 7%). This reflects NCBI's overall bias toward pathogen sequencing — clinical isolates tend to have good geographic metadata from epidemiological tracking, which is why they have AlphaEarth embeddings.
heading: 3. Strong clinical/human sampling bias in the AlphaEarth subset

text: The Other category contains 13,944 genomes (17%) and includes site-specific, generic, and clinical labels missed by keywords.
quote: An additional 13,944 genomes (17%) were classified as "Other" — site-specific labels (e.g., "Aspo HRL", "Olkiluoto" — underground research labs), generic terms ("water", "bodily fluid"), and clinical sites not captured by current keywords.
heading: 3. Strong clinical/human sampling bias in the AlphaEarth subset

text: A 2D UMAP projection of 64-dimensional embeddings yielded 320 DBSCAN clusters, many dominated by one environment category.
quote: UMAP reduction of the 64-dimensional embeddings to 2D reveals substantial structure. DBSCAN clustering identified 320 clusters. The cluster–environment cross-tabulation shows that many clusters are dominated by a single environment category:
heading: 5. UMAP reveals fine-grained embedding structure with environment-correlated clusters

text: Rare environment categories occupy a few clusters, whereas human gut and clinical categories span many; geographic substructure is an interpretation.
quote: Rare environment types (Air, Extreme, Plant) concentrate in just a few specific clusters, while common categories (Human gut, Human clinical) are distributed across many clusters — likely reflecting geographic sub-structure within those categories.
heading: 5. UMAP reveals fine-grained embedding structure with environment-correlated clusters

text: Apparent taxonomic clustering in UMAP is partly confounded with environment; the report gives gut-associated Campylobacterota as an example.
quote: Coloring the UMAP by phylum reveals some taxonomic clustering, though this is partially confounded with environment (e.g., Campylobacterota are predominantly gut-associated). The interactive HTML version (`figures/umap_by_phylum.html`) allows toggling phyla on/off to explore this structure.
heading: 6. Embedding space also shows taxonomic structure

text: AlphaEarth embeddings cover 83,287 of 293,059 genomes (28.4%); 79,449 have complete 64-dimensional values and 3,838 contain at least one NaN.
quote: The AlphaEarth embeddings table covers 83,287 genomes (28.4% of 293,059 total in the pangenome database). Of these, 79,449 have valid (non-NaN) embeddings across all 64 dimensions; 3,838 have NaN in at least one dimension.
heading: Data coverage

text: The report gives exact metadata coverage counts and percentages for cleaned coordinates, location name, isolation source, host, and three environment fields.
heading: Data coverage

text: The NCBI ncbi_env table contains 334 harmonized attributes across 4.1M rows, led by collection_date, geo_loc_name, and isolation_source.
quote: The NCBI `ncbi_env` table contains 334 distinct harmonized attribute names across 4.1M rows. The most populated are `collection_date` (273K genomes), `geo_loc_name` (272K), and `isolation_source` (245K).
heading: Data coverage

text: Keyword matching mapped 5,774 isolation-source values to 12 categories and captured 71% of genomes with a label; 17% remain Other and 12.5% Unknown.
quote: 5,774 unique `isolation_source` free-text values were mapped to 12 broad categories via keyword matching. The mapping captures 71% of genomes with a label; 17% remain as "Other" and 12.5% are "Unknown" (missing/null isolation_source).
heading: Environment harmonization

text: The ENVO env_broad_scale field covers only 42% of genomes and contains bare IDs or generic labels, although some terms are standardized.
quote: The `env_broad_scale` ENVO ontology field is cleaner but covers only 42% of genomes. Many values are bare ENVO IDs without labels (e.g., "ENVO:00000428") or generic terms ("not applicable", "missing"). Where available, structured ENVO terms like "marine biome [ENVO:00000447]" provide standardized categories.
heading: Environment harmonization

text: The 64 embedding dimensions range from -0.544 to 0.544, with mean -0.008 and mean standard deviation 0.109; embedded genomes span 135 phyla and 15,046 species.
quote: The 64 embedding dimensions (A00–A63) have values in [-0.544, 0.544], mean near zero (-0.008), mean standard deviation 0.109. The embeddings span 135 phyla, 15,046 species, and the full global extent (latitude -85 to +84, longitude -178 to +180).
heading: Embedding properties

text: AlphaEarth embeddings encode satellite-imagery-derived context at genome sampling locations; particular environmental features are interpretations.
quote: The embeddings encode **geographic/environmental context derived from satellite imagery** at each genome's sampling location. The strong geographic distance–embedding distance correlation (Finding 2) confirms they capture spatially varying environmental features — likely climate, land use, vegetation type, and urban/rural character.
heading: What do AlphaEarth embeddings represent?

text: The report interprets AlphaEarth embeddings as more informative for environmental microbiology samples than clinical isolates.
quote: The stratified analysis (Finding 1) reveals that the signal is primarily driven by variation in **natural environments**, not urban settings. Hospitals worldwide look similar from satellite; forests, oceans, and deserts do not. This has practical implications: the embeddings are most informative for environmental microbiology samples and least informative for clinical isolates.
heading: What do AlphaEarth embeddings represent?

text: A prior ecotype analysis found weak prediction of gene content from AlphaEarth similarity (median partial correlation 0.0025); clinical-bias dilution is proposed, not demonstrated here.
quote: The `ecotype_analysis` project previously found that AlphaEarth-based environment similarity was a weak predictor of gene content (median partial correlation 0.0025). The strong clinical bias identified here may partially explain that weak signal — if 38% of the genomes being compared are from interchangeable hospital environments, the environment–gene content relationship would be diluted. Repeating the ecotype analysis restricted to environmental samples could reveal a stronger signal.
heading: Implications for downstream analysis

text: The report cites Pearman et al. (2024) for environmental variation outweighing geographic separation in macroalgal microbiome composition.
quote: - Pearman et al. (2024) found that macroalgal microbiome composition responds primarily to **environmental variation rather than geographic separation**, supporting the "everything is everywhere, the environment selects" principle. Our stratified analysis (Finding 1) is consistent: the embeddings — which encode environmental conditions — show stronger distance-decay for environmental samples than for human-associated ones.
heading: Literature Context

text: The report cites Liu et al. (2022) for 4.16% variation explained by metal contamination versus 1.21% by geographic distance in mining-soil fungal communities.
quote: - Liu et al. (2022) showed that in mining soils, metal contamination explained more variation in fungal community structure (4.16%) than geographic distance (1.21%). Similarly, our data suggests the embeddings capture environmental features (land use, vegetation) more than raw distance, as evidenced by the plateau above ~5,000 km.
heading: Literature Context

text: The report cites Zhang et al. (2022) for similar distance-decay patterns but differing mechanisms in rare and abundant bacterial subcommunities.
quote: - Zhang et al. (2022) found that rare and abundant bacterial subcommunities show similar distance-decay patterns but differ mechanistically. Our finding that human-associated samples show weaker distance-decay echoes the idea that dispersal limitation (relevant for environmental microbes) generates stronger geographic patterns than deterministic selection alone.
heading: Literature Context

text: The report cites Wang et al. (2024) for aridity-shaped soil-bacterial biogeography and higher similarity-distance decay across environmental gradients.
quote: - Wang et al. (2024) demonstrated that aridity shapes distinct biogeographic patterns for soil bacteria, with higher similarity-distance decay rates across environmental gradients. This supports our interpretation that the AlphaEarth embeddings capture environmentally-driven variation.
heading: Literature Context

text: The report notes that pathogen and clinical-isolate bias in public genome databases can bias environment–genome analyses.
quote: The clinical sampling bias we identified (Finding 3) is a known issue in genomic databases but has not been quantified in the specific context of satellite-derived environmental embeddings. Public genome databases are heavily skewed toward pathogens and clinical isolates (Saha et al., 2023), which biases any analysis of environment-genome relationships.
heading: Literature Context

text: AlphaEarth coverage is limited to 28.4% of genomes and biased toward valid coordinate metadata.
quote: - **AlphaEarth coverage is only 28.4%** of all genomes — biased toward those with valid lat/lon metadata
heading: Limitations

text: The 38% clinical/human composition may not represent the overall NCBI or pangenome population.
quote: - **Clinical/human bias (38%)** may not represent the overall NCBI or pangenome population
heading: Limitations

text: Coordinate QC falsely flags some legitimate field sites and needs isolation-source homogeneity checks.
quote: - **Coordinate QC heuristic is crude** — flags some legitimate field sites (Rifle, Saanich Inlet); needs refinement using isolation_source homogeneity
heading: Limitations

text: Keyword-based harmonization leaves 17% Other and misses site-specific or non-English labels.
quote: - **Environment harmonization has a long tail** — 17% "Other" category; keyword matching doesn't capture site-specific labels or non-English terms
heading: Limitations

text: UMAP clusters depend on n_neighbors and min_dist and may not reflect high-dimensional embedding topology.
quote: - **UMAP is a non-linear projection** — cluster structure depends on parameters (n_neighbors, min_dist) and may not reflect true high-dimensional topology
heading: Limitations

text: Embedding NaNs affect 4.6% of records; their cause is unknown.
quote: - **Embedding NaN values (4.6%)** — cause unknown; possibly missing satellite imagery at those coordinates
heading: Limitations

text: DBSCAN at eps=0.5 produced 320 clusters, which the report considers likely too fine-grained for environment categories.
quote: - **DBSCAN eps=0.5 produced 320 clusters** — likely too fine-grained; coarser clustering may better match environment categories
heading: Limitations
